samples.text:
Climate change is a global problem which affect every country in the world. Some people think that rich countries should pay most of the money to solve it, but other people believe all countries should pay the same. In this essay I will look at both sides and give my opinion.

On the one hand, there are good reasons for wealthy countries to pay more. These countries started to use factories and cars much earlier than other nations, so they have produced most of the pollution in the past. Also, they have more money and better technology, so it is easier for them to pay. In contrast, many poor countries are still trying to provide basic things like electricity and clean water for its people, so they cannot spend a lot on climate problems.

On the other hand, some people argue that everyone should pay equally. Today, some developing countries, especially big ones, produce a large amount of pollution because their industries are growing fast. If only rich countries pay, these countries may not try to reduce the emissions. Furthermore, climate change will affect all of us, so it seem fair that every country share the responsibility.

In my opinion, rich countries should pay the most of the cost, but other countries should also do something. Wealthy nations caused more of the problem and they have more money. However, developing countries should also make promises to reduce pollution, according to what they can afford.

In conclusion, both views have reasons. I believe that the wealthy countries should pay more because it is fairer, but all countries must work together to stop climate change.
samples.why: All parts addressed with a clear opinion · relevant main ideas but underdeveloped · basic, repetitive linking · adequate but plain vocabulary · several agreement, pronoun and article errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Tackling climate change will require enormous investment, and there is disagreement over how this burden should be distributed. Some believe that wealthy nations should cover most of the cost, while others argue that every country should contribute equally. In my opinion, richer countries should pay the larger share, although all nations must play some part.

The case for wealthy countries paying more rests on both history and capacity. Industrialised nations have been burning fossil fuels for over two centuries, so they are responsible for a large proportion of the greenhouse gases already in the atmosphere. They have also benefited economically from this development. Furthermore, they have the financial resources and technical expertise to fund clean energy projects, whereas many poorer countries are struggling to provide basic services such as healthcare and electricity for their citizens.

Those who support equal contributions, however, raise valid points. Several fast-growing economies are now among the largest emitters, and if they are not required to pay, there may be little incentive for them to limit their emissions. Some also argue that since climate change threatens everyone, every country has an equal interest in solving it and should therefore carry an equal responsibility. There is a concern too that citizens in rich countries may be unwilling to support policies which appear to place the whole burden on them.

On balance, I believe that an equal split would be unfair and unrealistic. Asking a low-income country to pay the same as a wealthy one ignores huge differences in wealth and historical responsibility. A better system would be based on a combination of past emissions and current income, so that each country contributes in proportion to it's ability and impact.

In conclusion, although all nations share the consequences of climate change, the costs of tackling it should fall mainly on wealthy countries, with developing countries contributing according to their means.
samples.why: Clear position throughout · both views extended and supported · coherent paragraphs with a range of linking devices · good topic vocabulary (emitters, historical responsibility) · mostly accurate complex sentences with one minor slip.

samples.text:
As the costs of addressing climate change mount, so does the question of who should bear them. One view holds that wealthy nations should shoulder most of the financial burden; another insists that the costs should be divided equally among all countries. I believe that a fair arrangement must reflect differences in both responsibility and capacity, which means that richer countries should pay considerably more.

The argument for placing the main burden on wealthy countries is rooted in historical responsibility. The nations that industrialised first have emitted the bulk of the carbon dioxide that has accumulated in the atmosphere, and their current prosperity was built, in large part, on that fossil-fuel-driven growth. It therefore seems just that they should now fund a substantial share of the transition. They are also far better placed to do so, possessing the capital, infrastructure and research capacity that many developing countries lack.

Advocates of equal contributions nevertheless make a case that deserves serious consideration. Emissions are no longer concentrated in the traditional industrial powers; several rapidly developing economies now produce a significant proportion of global emissions. Exempting them from financial responsibility could weaken their commitment to decarbonisation and breed resentment among taxpayers in wealthier states. Moreover, since climate change threatens every country, some would argue that a shared problem demands an equally shared solution.

In my view, however, treating unequal nations equally would itself be inequitable. Requiring a country where much of the population lacks reliable electricity to contribute as much as one of the world's richest economies would hinder its development while doing little for the climate. A more defensible approach would scale contributions according to historical emissions, current emissions and national income, ensuring that every country participates while the heaviest costs fall on those most able to bear them.

In conclusion, although all nations have a stake in combating climate change, fairness requires that wealthy countries fund the greater part of the effort, with others contributing in proportion to their means.
samples.why: Both positions thoroughly explored and weighed · sophisticated, well-justified opinion · excellent logical progression and cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (inequitable, decarbonisation) · wide range of complex structures, error-free.
